<reason>Both sides argued a genuine, coherent clash and both handled the pressure round honestly with proper A1/A2 structure. CON's route was the "missing predicate" distinction: past act or present clinical finding versus a forecast. PRO's route was the least-restrictive-means comparison plus asymmetric error costs. PRO won the exchange because (1) its sister hypothetical forced CON to name an alternative, and CON's answer—emergency detention, then "more treatment or an extended commitment"—let PRO show CON's toolkit is more intrusive (seize the person) yet never touches the lethal object; (2) CON's honest "Yes, I would still oppose it" under maximal safeguards neutralized its own opening arguments about custody fights, heated texts, and false positives, narrowing CON to a categorical claim that pre-conviction removal is never permissible; and (3) PRO's calendar-versus-funeral weighing, while CON rightly noted it presumes the forecast is true, still accounted for the false-positive case in a way CON's "undefended nights" did not fully rebut. CON's reframing of psychiatric holds as "present incapacity" rather than prediction was its best move but somewhat strained, since such holds are also danger-based. PRO's three clipped turns are a real execution cost and keep the margin competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1/A-side follow-through on the sister hypothetical: after CON offered emergency detention as the existing tool, PRO asked what remains when the 72-hour hold ends and the rifle is still in the house. CON's answer—extended commitment—let PRO crystallize the closing line that CON's rule lets "the state take your body but never your cabinet," turning CON's least-intrusive claim inside out.</best_rebuttal>
